title: Unit-sum mechanism over Z: the only integer e are 1 and 2 — consequence: classes 3 and 2 mod 4 only
connection: Over ℕ, 1/u + 1/v ∈ Z forces e ∈ {1, 2}, giving the classical easy classes. Any p-dependent replacement must produce e = 1/u + 1/v with u, v rational but with x = (n+e)/4 integer — i.e. e may depend on p.
why: Pins down the precise integer statement replacing the universal divisor: 'for every p there is e ≡ 3 mod 4 with e = 1/u+1/v and u·n·x, v·n·x integers' — which is ES itself in e-slice form.

title: Chain world (x | y | z): every failure is ≡ 1 (mod 24), and 161 of the 267 such primes fail

title: Normal-form lemma (proved): in every solution x ≤ y ≤ z of 4/p (p odd prime), p divides z
connection: Proof: x ≤ 3p/4 < p so p ∤ x; reducing mod p forces p | y or p | z. Suppose p ∤ z, y = pb: then (4b−1)xz = pb(x+z) so 4b−1 = pt; with a = 4x−p > 0 one gets z = pbx/(ab−x), and z ≥ pb gives x < ab ≤ 2x, hence t ≤ 1/p + 2/a; a ≥ 3 is impossible for odd p, and a = 1 forces t = 1, b = x, contradicting ab > x (proof completed by the review subagent). Data: all 21 909 solutions for p < 2500 checked directly; share check at all primes ≤ 10⁵.
why: Explains minz(p) ≡ 0 (mod p) and gives a normal form ('z-anchored') for all ES solutions at primes — useful for parametrisations; it says nothing about existence.
first_step: Record as a lemma; check it is ET's Type I/II dichotomy in disguise (k₁ ↔ only z divisible, k₂ ↔ y, z divisible).

connection: Type I: f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd. Many samples p² + 4c²d (varying c,d) each near a multiple of an unknown f is the 'approximate GCD' setting from homomorphic encryption; its hardness/easiness results describe when such common divisors exist.

title: p-adic Hensel-lifting view: ES at p is a statement about the p-adic unit 4/p... no — about x,y,z with exactly one or two divisible by p (Type I/II)
connection: Type I: p | x only; write x = pX. Then 4/p = 1/(pX) + 1/y + 1/z ⟹ (4X − 1)/(pX) = 1/y + 1/z. So Type I ⟺ (4X−1)/(pX) is a two-term Egyptian fraction for some X. Type II: x = pX, y = pY: 4/p − 1/(pX) − 1/(pY) = (4XY − X − Y)/(pXY) = 1/z ⟹ z = pXY/(4XY − X − Y): Type II ⟺ (4XY − X − Y) | pXY. Since gcd(4XY−X−Y, XY) | ... these are the 'words' p = tuv − u − v? Let me not resolve; the item: make the X-parametrisations the primary object and study the p-adic valuations.
why: Explicit small-parameter forms (X, Y) make 'Type II ⟺ ∃ X,Y: (4XY − X − Y) | pXY' which with gcd analysis becomes 4XY − X − Y = p·(divisor of XY)/... The repo's word form p = tuv − u − v is this. Keep as the 'word' entry point for the free lane.

title: Odd squares m² are uncovered by the (C, a) covering system — turn this into a *characterisation* of uncovered integers
connection: T1 says no Type I/II solutions at odd squares; in the covering language, m² ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod a with a ≡ −1 mod 4C never holds (reciprocity). Ask: are odd squares the ONLY uncovered integers (together with the U(n) sporadics 105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145 — which concern a related but different U(n) statement; check which)? If the uncovered set is exactly {odd squares} ∪ finite, then ES is 'covering system misses exactly the squares', a Rickards–Stange-type statement.

Here moduli repeat? (Different C can give the same a: a ≡ −1 mod 4C and mod 4C′ means lcm | a + 1.)

title: Does T1 kill (u, v)-identities? Check what happens to a (u,v)-polynomial identity at p = m² = u² + v²
connection: If an identity in (u,v) valid for all coprime (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 existed, it would produce Type I/II solutions for m² whenever m² = u² + v² with gcd(u,v) = 1 and uv ≠ 0 — which happens iff m has a prime factor ≡ 1 mod 4 (Pythagorean). T1 says no such solution exists ⟹ NO (u,v)-polynomial identity can be valid on all coprime (u,v) with the right residues. So (u,v)-identities must also exclude Pythagorean (u,v) — i.e. must depend on more than residues of (u,v). Record as a lemma killing the naive version; the surviving version needs a non-polynomial ingredient (e.g. gcd or primality of u² + v²).
why: Saves a wasted search; and pinpoints the 'Pythagorean' loophole: an identity could be valid only when u² + v² is not a square — but polynomial identities can't 'know' that. Same for u² + 2v², etc. (m² = u² + 2v² has solutions when m has a factor ≡ 1,3 mod 8).
first_step: Write the lemma; then ask: are there identities in (u,v) valid for all (u,v) with u² + v² ≡ 1 mod 24 EXCEPT where u² + v² is a square — impossible for polynomials; so the item above (Gaussian identities) is dead in its polynomial form; keep only residue-branching + non-polynomial variants.

Computation (p < 20000, d < 1500): the only prime ≡ 1 (mod 4) without such a certificate is 2521 (= 3·840 + 1, in the Mordell-hard class 1 mod 840); 409, 577, 5569, 9601 are certified by (d, f) = (11, 75), (5, 3), (17, 7), (67, 851). Conversely 2521 is not a C-form exception. So the two one-parameter forms have disjoint exceptional sets in this range and their union covers everything.

Both exception types are now concrete test cases for any mechanism.

title: The C-form as a statement about shifted primes: ES(p) ⟸ ∃u ≥ 1 with a divisor of p + u congruent to −1 (mod 4u) — compare with the theory of divisors of shifted primes (Erdős, Hooley's Δ-function, Ford's divisors in intervals)
connection: Given the reparametrisation (previous item), the C-form says: among p + 1, p + 2, …, some p + u has a divisor in the class −1 mod 4u. The divisor structure of shifted primes p + u (for fixed u, varying p) is classical (Erdős: p + 1 has typically log log p factors, the arcsine law holds for its divisors — Hall–Tenenbaum). The new twist: u varies with p fixed — the 'horizontal' direction again; Hooley's Δ-function and Ford's 'divisors in intervals' concern how divisors of a single integer are spread; here we need, for each u, a divisor of p + u near a specific residue class mod 4u — i.e., a divisor a with a ≡ −1 (4u); equivalently (a + 1)/4u ∈ ℤ, so a + 1 is a multiple of 4u while a divides p + u.
why: Reformulation puts ES into the well-developed 'divisors of shifted integers' literature (Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors'), with the familiar polylog count: E[#{u ≤ X : p + u has a divisor ≡ −1 (4u)}] ≈ Σ_u τ(p+u)/φ(4u) ≈ log p · log X. The pointwise question is identical but now 'horizontal in u' with additive shifts — the Hardy–Littlewood/Dickson flavour.
first_step: Verify the reparametrisation (bijection between (C, u, v) and (u, a)), then search Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors' for any theorem about divisors of n + u in a class depending on u (probably none); formulate the cleanest statement: 'for every non-square n ≥ 2 there is u ≥ 1 and a | n + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u)' — FALSE for n = 409 (if the C ≤ 60000 search transfers: u ≤ 60000).
refs: Ford, 'The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval' (Ann. Math 2008)

title: Type I in the shifted form: f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) — is there an analogous 'p + u has a divisor in a class' statement for Type I (c = 1: f | p² + 4d, f ≡ −p mod 4d)?
connection: By analogy with the C-form reparametrisation, Type I c = 1 should be expressible as 'some pu + 1 (or p·u + something) has a divisor in a class'. From the e-slice form: Type I ↔ N = (pe + 1)/4 — multiplicative shift pe + 1; Type II ↔ N = (p + e)/4 — additive shift. So the two types are 'additive shifts p + e' and 'multiplicative shifts pe + 1' of p, each needing a divisor in a tied class. The C-form (p + u with divisor ≡ −1 mod 4u) is the additive one; Type I c=1 should be: pe + 1 has a divisor ≡ (something) mod 4e... Derive precisely.
why: A symmetric 'additive vs multiplicative shift' picture of the two types is a memorable organising principle, and the exceptions (409 fails additive; 2521 fails multiplicative) become 'a prime for which all additive shifts fail' vs 'all multiplicative shifts fail'. Both one-parameter statements are false for some primes; ES says the two never fail together (empirically).
first_step: Derive the Type I c=1 shifted statement from FRONTIER's e-slice form; verify numerically on 2521 (which e's fail and why); write the symmetric table.

title: Hypothesis: 409 is obstructed because every divisor a of p + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) must satisfy (a/p) = −1 AND a ≡ −u^{-1}·... — derive the second forced symbol in the shifted form
connection: In the shifted form a | p + u ⟹ p ≡ −u (mod a) ⟹ (p/a) = (−u/a) = (−1/a)(u/a) = −(u/a) (a ≡ 3 mod 4); also a ≡ −1 (mod 4u) ⟹ (u/a) = +1 by reciprocity (as before for C) ⟹ (p/a) = −1 ⟹ (a/p) = −1. Same forced symbol. Now also consider (u/p): from a | p + u, nothing forces (u/p). Hmm; but the cofactor b = (p+u)/a satisfies... In the C-form, the cofactor was ≡ −1 mod 4C too; in the shifted form the cofactor b = (p + u)/a — its class mod 4u? p + u ≡ ? mod 4u: p ≡ 1 mod 4, so p + u mod 4u is p + u — not controlled. So in the shifted form the cofactor is unconstrained — then the (u, a) ↔ (C, a, b) bijection must impose b ≡ ... let me recheck: from 4Cp + 1 = ab, a = 4Cu − 1: b = (4Cp + 1)/(4Cu − 1); with the claim 'a | p + u': 4Cp + 1 ≡ 0 (mod a) and 4Cu ≡ 1 (mod a) ⟹ 4Cp ≡ −1 ⟹ multiply by u: 4Cu·p ≡ −u ⟹ p ≡ −u (mod a) ✓. Conversely a | p + u with a ≡ −1 (mod 4u): set 4Cu = a + 1 (C = (a+1)/(4u) ∈ ℤ ✓), then 4Cp = (a+1)p/u ≡ ? We need a | 4Cp + 1: 4Cp + 1 = ((a+1)p + u)/u; mod a: (p + u)/u ≡ 0 ✓ (since a | p + u and gcd(a, u) = 1 as a ≡ −1 mod u). So b = (4Cp+1)/a is an integer and b ≡ ? mod 4C: ab = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1, a ≡ −1 ⟹ b ≡ −1 ✓ automatically. Good: the bijection holds with no extra condition. So the shifted form is exactly right: C-form ⟺ ∃u: (p + u) has a divisor ≡ −1 (mod 4u).
why: Confirms the reparametrisation rigorously (no hidden cofactor condition) and shows the only forced symbol is (a/p) = −1; so 409's obstruction, if structural, is not a second Jacobi symbol of this simple type — it must involve the interplay of a ≡ −1 (4u), a | 409 + u across u.
first_step: Record the proof; then compute for 409 the set of 'near misses': u ≤ 10⁴ and divisors a of 409 + u with a ≡ −1 mod 4u′ for the largest u′ | u-ish — see how close the condition comes to being satisfied.

connection: Markov and ES share F13,F14,F38: cubic surfaces with coordinate symmetry and involutive transformations. Markov’s mutation gives a concrete comparison to ES’s fixed-fibre hyperbola involution.

connection: The divisor-sum formulation shares F10, F15, F21, F29: an ES witness exists iff a p-tied integer has a divisor in a prescribed residue class (this sub-problem is open, not solved).

title: Prime gaps and thin algebraic sequences

title: Davenport–Lewis–Schinzel / Cassels–Pfister: polynomial-identity theorems for sums of squares ↔ Mordell–Schinzel for ES
connection: Davenport–Lewis–Schinzel: if f ∈ ℤ[t] and f(n) is a sum of two squares for every n, then f is a sum of two squares of polynomials; Cassels–Pfister: a polynomial that is a sum of k squares of rational functions is a sum of k squares of polynomials. These are the sums-of-squares analogues of 'no polynomial identity covers the square classes' (F09).
why: Shows how polynomial-identity impossibility is proved by valuation/specialisation arguments; could give a uniform proof of F09 and its extensions (identities in two parameters, Gaussian coordinates).

title: Merikoski largest prime factor of n²+1 → ES Type I values p²+4c²d
connection: Merikoski (JEMS 2023) shows P⁺(n²+1) > n^{1.279} using Deshouillers–Iwaniec Kloosterman bounds on divisors of n²+1 in ranges; ES Type I needs a divisor of p²+4c²d in a specific class and range.

title: Bilu–Tichy / Hilbert irreducibility for 'identity families' over ℚ(t)
connection: Bilu–Tichy classify when f(x) = g(y) has infinitely many integral solutions; ES identity families are polynomial solutions; Hilbert irreducibility explains when parametric families give integral specialisations.

title: Additive basis view of I3: tuv−u−v as a 'thin basis' of order 1 with three free parameters
connection: The set W₃ = {tuv − u − v : t,u,v ≥ 3} has counting function ≍ N (it is almost everything), but the representation function is only ≍ log²n. Thin-basis theory (Erdős–Tetali; Nathanson) studies bases with small representation functions.
why: Erdős–Tetali gives random bases with r(n) ≍ log n that are bases for all large n. Deterministic thin bases with full coverage are rare; I3 would be a natural deterministic example.
first_step: Survey known deterministic 'thin bases' with polylog representation functions and full coverage; check whether any proof technique applies to multiplicative shapes.
refs: Erdős–Tetali, Representations of integers as the sum of k terms (1990)

title: Adversarial factorisation game: the only link between levels is CRT consistency
connection: Model: an adversary assigns factorisations to the integers 4Cp+1 (all C) consistently with every congruence p satisfies. ES is the claim that no consistent assignment avoids all certificates. Barrier theorems in the repo are exactly 'consistent avoiding assignments exist for the abstract model'.
why: It locates precisely what a proof must use beyond CRT consistency: the actual multiplicative structure (that the integers really are 4Cp + 1 for one p).
first_step: Write down the minimal 'consistency axioms' satisfied by real factorisations (e.g. gcd(4Cp+1, 4C′p+1) | 4(C−C′)… and the sizes) that the abstract model violates; any such axiom is a candidate proof ingredient.

title: Subspace-theorem methods for divisibility relations (Corvaja–Zannier)
connection: Roth → Schmidt's subspace theorem → Corvaja–Zannier results on divisibility a^n − 1 | b^n − 1 and on S-integral points. ES is a divisibility relation (4uC − 1) | (p + u); the subspace theorem controls such relations in exponential/algebraic families.

title: Arithmetic constructions cover some classes, interlacing covers all: the LPS → MSS lesson
connection: LPS/Morgenstern built Ramanujan graphs arithmetically only for degrees d − 1 = prime power; MSS proved existence for every d by a non-arithmetic existence method (interlacing families). ES: Mordell identities (arithmetic) cover all non-square classes mod 840; the square classes may need a non-identity existence method of a comparable kind.

refs: arXiv:1304.4132 (Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava, Interlacing families I: all degrees)

title: Chebyshev-type explicit bounds for the certificate-capable prime mass
connection: Chebyshev proved x/log x-type bounds for π(x) by explicit factorial inequalities. Define the 'certificate-capable prime mass' Θ_p(K) = Σ_{q certificate-capable at some C ≤ K} log q and try to prove Chebyshev-type explicit lower bounds for it at fixed p using only CRT structure of Π_C(4Cp + 1).

title: Exact formulas for divisor-class counts: Ramanujan sums expansion of D_C^−(N)
connection: Rademacher-type exact expansions use Kloosterman/Ramanujan sums. The class-restricted divisor count D^−_{4C}(N) has an exact finite Fourier expansion over additive characters mod 4C (Ramanujan sums c_q(·)); for the all-level sum this becomes a series Σ_q c_q-type terms, an ES 'singular series' with exact tail.
why: An exact Ramanujan-sum expansion of R(p) separates the main (BM) part from the rest explicitly and may be summable in closed form at small q.
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_q A_q(p) with A_q built from Ramanujan sums; compute A_q(p) numerically for q ≤ 100 and the remainder.

title: Linear recurrences for minimal certificates along exponential families
connection: SML-type structure suggests that along n_s = a·b^s + c the minimal certificate parameters may follow linear recurrences in s on residue classes of s. Detect such recurrences for the proved families (3·2^s + 1, 63·2^s + 1) and use them to predict certificates for open families.
why: Recurrences would give explicit every-s constructions (as Niederreiter for Zaremba).
first_step: Run Berlekamp–Massey on sequences of minimal (u, B, C) along proved families restricted to s in fixed classes.

title: Keating–Rudnick variance in F_q[T] as model for the variance of Type II counts over C
connection: Variance of arithmetic functions in FF arithmetic progressions is computed exactly via random matrix theory for q → ∞. The fixed-p ES count Σ_C #(divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C) is a sum of divisor-in-AP indicators.

first_step: Check whether Keating–Rudnick 'squarefree / divisor function in arithmetic progressions over F_q[T]' covers d(n) restricted to a class; adapt to the Type II sum at q→∞.

title: Lang–Weil/Ax ultraproduct of F_q[T]: ES in a pseudo-finite polynomial ring
connection: The ultraproduct of F_q[T] over q has a pseudo-finite constant field; ES over it is decided by Lang–Weil point counts on the fixed-degree ES variety, giving failure (Thm 2.1) for standard degree.

title: Mason–Stothers in F_q[T] vs abc over Z for size of largest ES denominator
connection: abc is a theorem in F_q[T] (Mason–Stothers, under the usual hypothesis that not all of a, b, c have zero derivative — i.e. excluding p-th-power cases like T^p + (1 − T)^p = 1); applied to ES identities it bounds degrees of solutions. Over Z, abc would bound sizes of x,y,z from below/above in terms of rad(xyz·n).
why: Size bounds feed every search strategy; an FF theorem with its Z-conditional twin may reveal a forced-size window for solutions.

title: Identity for 4/(S²+T²) restricted to a cone avoiding Pythagorean pairs
connection: Primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) are exactly the primes S² + T². A Z[S,T] identity valid on a cone would prove ES for the primes in it; Mordell–Schinzel-type obstruction bites at (S,T) with S²+T² a square (Pythagorean pairs).

title: ES over F_q[T] for P = composite: does the reduction to primes hold?
connection: Over Z, ES for n follows from ES for any divisor of n. Over F_q[T] the same divisor-closure holds, but FF exceptions may be prime-only; check if all composite exceptions inherit from prime factors.

title: Function-field Chen-type theorem: P + E = (almost prime)·(...) in classes
connection: Chen-type 'almost prime' results are proved in FF with better parameters. The e-slice criterion needs a divisor of P·x-type polynomial in a class; an almost-prime shift result constrains which certificate exists.
why: If FF almost-prime results make ES-type certificate existence automatic, the integer twin would be a Chen-type ES theorem ('p+e has ≤ 2 prime factors with one in class').

title: Integer-valued polynomial ring Int(Z) as denominators
connection: Allow X_i(T) ∈ Int(Z) = {f ∈ Q[T]: f(Z) ⊆ Z} (binomial-coefficient basis). This strictly enlarges the identity world beyond Z[T].
why: Mordell–Schinzel's proof might use integrality of coefficients; if it breaks for Int(Z), new identity families covering harder classes might exist (though T1 at squares should still bite pointwise).

title: Quasi-polynomial identities (periodic coefficients) = finite coverings
connection: Allowing coefficients periodic in T is the same as finitely many polynomial identities on classes, so the quasi-polynomial world is equivalent to the B1 covering world (and fails at square classes).
why: Useful as a boundary marker: any 'identity' approach that is quasi-polynomial is already excluded.

title: Positive ES over Z[1/ℓ] for EVERY odd prime ℓ (unit-sum mechanism; checked ℓ < 3000)
connection: Over Z[1/ℓ] the mechanism of other_rings Lemma 3.1 works iff some 1 + ℓ^k has a prime factor ≡ 3 (mod 4). scripts/z52b_analogues_zl.py: every odd prime ℓ < 3000 has such k ≤ 7 (max at ℓ = 2017). A reciprocity argument shows failure for all odd k would force ℓ ≡ 1 (mod 8). (NB: for ℓ with ES(ℓ) known, Z[1/ℓ]-ES is even more trivial by the depth-1 identity of the next item; the unit mechanism matters as an ES-independent proof.)
why: Turns Prop 3.2 (ℓ = 3) into a uniform theorem over all Z[1/ℓ] with a proof independent of ES itself; records exactly what 'one inverted prime' buys.

title: Depth-1 trivialization: denominators in (1/ℓ)·ℕ make ES trivial whenever ES(ℓ) holds
connection: 4/n = Σ ℓ/x'_i ⇔ 4/(ℓn) = Σ 1/x'_i, and ES(ℓn) follows from ES(ℓ). E.g. ℓ = 3: 4/n = 1/(n/3) + 1/(4n/3) + 1/(4n) for every n. So the 'ℓ-adic depth' hierarchy collapses at depth 1 (k(p) ∈ {0,1}); Prop 3.2's e = 7 identity (depth 3) is not optimal. Likewise ℓ = 2: 4/n = Σ 2/x' ⇔ 2/n = Σ 1/x', trivial.
why: Correction/sharpening of the S-integer picture: the meaningful refinement is not depth but HOW MANY denominators are non-integral (the trivial identity uses two). 'Exactly one non-integral denominator of ℓ-depth 1' is weighted ES with weights (1,1,ℓ), trivial for ℓ ≤ 3 (take z = n) and non-trivial for ℓ ≥ 5.
first_step: Done cheaply: scripts/z52b_analogues_weighted.py finds NO failure of 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + ℓ/z (ℓ ∤ z, z ≤ 3p) for ℓ = 5, 7, 11 and p < 3000. So every single non-unit numerator seems to make ES easy (expected: e.g. 4z − 5p = 3 leaves 3/(pz)). Next: find the uniform identity per ℓ and record the lemma.

title: Inverting the target prime trivializes ES: positive ES over Z[1/p] for 4/p
connection: In Z[1/p] the unit-sum mechanism applies with ℓ = p itself: if some 1 + p^k has a divisor e ≡ 3 (mod 4) (true for all p < 3000 by the Z[1/ℓ] computation) then 4/p = 1/x + 1/(u p x) + 1/(v p x), x = (p+e)/4. So allowing p-power denominators removes the obstruction; e.g. 4/5 uses e = 3 | 1 + 5.
why: Localizes the difficulty: allowing p-power denominators kills it. (Depth-1 with ℓ = p is circular — it needs ES(p²) — so the unit route is the honest one here.)

title: Matrix ES with commuting denominators reduces to number-field ES
connection: If X, Y, Z commute, they lie in a commutative order (a product of number-field orders), so matrix ES with commuting denominators ⇔ ES over products of orders with the totally-positive cone.
why: Shows the matrix world's novelty must come from non-commuting solutions; commuting ones are already covered by the number-field items.

title: ν(p) ≤ 1 trivially: 4/p = 1/(p/3) + 1/(2p) + 1/(2p) — one non-integral denominator always suffices
connection: Define ν(p) = least number of non-integral denominators in a positive S-integer solution. Then ν(p) ≤ 1 for every p via 4/p − 3/p = 1/p = 1/(2p) + 1/(2p). ES ⇔ ν(p) = 0. So the S-integer relaxations collapse completely: any single non-unit numerator suffices.
why: Filter lemma: the entire S-integer/weighted direction gives no intermediate statement between 'trivial' and ES; the only non-trivial content of the S-integer worlds is the unit-sum MECHANISM (e | 1 + η), not the relaxation itself.
first_step: Record as a filter lemma; redirect S-integer effort to finding integer surrogates of η (p-tied 'units').
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Matrix ES for n·I replaced by a matrix of determinant n
connection: Ask: for every integral M with det M = n (or Hermite normal form), is 4M⁻¹ = X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ with X, Y, Z positive-definite integral? For M = diag(1, n) it contains ES-like constraints in one coordinate.
why: Gives a family indexed by sublattices of index n; averaging over sublattices might be easier and still imply ES for M = n^{1/k}-free choices.
first_step: Work out k = 2, M = diag(1, p): what does positivity + integrality force on the (2,2) coordinate?
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES in Z × Z (product ring) with componentwise positivity: no coupling
connection: In a product ring ES holds iff it holds in each factor. Trivial, but it calibrates: coupling between places is what makes rings like O_K differ from Z × Z.
why: A boundary marker for the cone-classification theorem.
first_step: Note as a one-line lemma in the dictionary.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over the ring of S-integers with S = {∞, 2-adic}? (Z[1/2]) vs S = {∞, 3}: compare collapse mechanisms
connection: Z[1/2]: trivial because 4 is a unit; Z[1/3]: needs e = 7 | 1 + 27. These are two different collapse mechanisms (numerator becomes unit vs universal divisor).
why: Distinguishes two kinds of 'easy' worlds; an integer proof might mimic the second (divisor supply) but never the first.
first_step: List all S-integer rings with |S| = 1 and classify which mechanism applies (done for ℓ < 3000 by the Zsigmondy item).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Integer consequence of the Z[1/ℓ] world is circular (ES(ℓn) ⇐ ES(ℓ)) — only the unit mechanism gives non-circular content
connection: Clearing ℓ-denominators from a Z[1/ℓ]-solution yields an integer representation of 4ℓ^k/n with ℓ-weighted terms; for the depth-1 identity this is just ES(ℓ)·(1/n). Hence S-integer worlds transfer to Z only through mechanisms not using ES(ℓ) — i.e. the unit-sum mechanism (e | 1 + ℓ^k).
why: Filters out a false lead: 'S-integer ES ⇒ integer Schinzel statement' is empty unless the S-integer proof is unit-driven.
first_step: Record as a filter lemma in the S-integer section; check that no repo memo claims a non-trivial integer consequence of Z[1/3]-ES.

title: Squarefree denominators: never fails for p < 4000 — conjecture ES with squarefree x, y, z
connection: The constrained world 'all denominators squarefree' had a solution at every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 (also cube-free, pairwise non-coprime, distinct).
why: A strictly stronger conjecture that seems true can be a better proof target if squarefreeness gives extra structure (e.g. Möbius sieving directly over squarefree parameters).
first_step: Extend to 10^6 (cheap with a smarter search); if no failures, formulate 'ES_sqf' and check how Type II parameters (a,b,c,d) must look for squarefree output.

areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: At least one denominator prime: fails at 93 of 269 primes below 4000
connection: Requiring some denominator to be prime (often p itself, i.e. 3/p = 1/y + 1/z) fails frequently: p = 37, 73, 97, 193, …. With x = p it is the 2-term problem 3/p = 1/y + 1/z, solvable iff p has... (p prime: iff p ≡ 2 mod 3).
why: Explains a large part of the failure structure via a known 2-term criterion and shows the role of 'Type I with x = p'.
first_step: Check: failures ⊆ {p ≡ 1 mod 3}? and the remaining prime-denominator solutions with a prime ≠ p — classify.

areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Weighted ES: 4/n = a/x + b/y + c/z for fixed weight vectors (a,b,c)
connection: A whole family of ternary problems indexed by (a,b,c). (1,1,2) is trivial (previous item); (1,1,1) is ES. Which weight vectors are 'hard' (lottery) vs 'trivial' (identity covering) vs 'false'?
why: The hard/trivial boundary in weight space exposes what feature of (1,1,1) creates difficulty (e.g. no weight shares a factor with 4).
first_step: Brute-force n ≤ 10^4 for all (a,b,c) with a,b,c ≤ 4 and classify by existence of a finite covering by identities mod 840.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Distinctness is harmless: the 'distinct' world never fails (p < 4000)
connection: Every p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 4000 has a solution with x, y, z distinct. Folklore says distinctness is WLOG for n > 2.
why: Confirms a reduction used everywhere; worth a one-line lemma (split a repeated term) to remove any doubt.
first_step: Write the splitting lemma: if x = y then 2/x = 1/(x/2)... or use 1/x = 1/(x+1) + 1/(x(x+1)) with care to keep 3 terms; check the literature statement.

title: ES with denominators restricted to a numerical semigroup or to values of a polynomial
connection: E.g. denominators of the form k(k+1) (pronic) telescope: 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k − 1/(k+1). ES with pronic denominators is a strongly restricted world with a telescoping algebra.
why: Telescoping algebras convert sums into differences, i.e. into signed problems; the pronic world might be equivalent to a signed ES with special structure.
first_step: Brute force n ≤ 10^4 for pronic and triangular denominators; derive the equivalence with signed sums.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Quasi-homogeneous relaxations: lct of x^a y + y^b + z^c is (a + b − 1)/(ab) + 1/c
connection: For f = x^a y + y^b + z^c, weights w_y = 1/b, w_x = (b − 1)/(ab), w_z = 1/c give lct = Σ w = (a+b−1)/(ab) + 1/c (if ≤ 1). Each Arnold/Orlik–Wagreich type gives a 'generalized Egyptian' expression for rationals.
why: A family of ES-like problems with a geometric origin; if one type (e.g. chain x^a y + y^b z + z^c) represents every 4/n, it is a provable relaxation and its proof might be adapted.
first_step: Derive the weight-sum formulas for the 7 Orlik–Wagreich-type classes of 3-variable isolated quasi-homogeneous singularities and test which represent 4/p for all p ≤ 10^4.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hurwitz existence problem for branched covers with three branch points
connection: A degree-N cover of S² branched over 3 points with all ramification orders x, y, z respectively (uniform data) exists iff Riemann–Hurwitz integrality holds plus combinatorial conditions; for ES triples the data have χ = N(4/n − 1).
why: Mostly the arithmetic is ES itself; but non-uniform branch data (mixing orders) give relaxations '4/n = average of reciprocals' that are solvable, a new interpolating family.
first_step: Formulate 'ES with averaged reciprocals' (branch data with different ramification orders above each point) and check if it is always solvable.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: No denominator ≡ 1 (mod 3): fails only at p = 5, 13, 37, 97 below 2·10^4
connection: Requiring all denominators to avoid the class 1 mod 3 fails at only four small primes. This 3-adic constrained world is almost as complete as ES.
why: A '3-adic strengthening' with finitely many exceptions suggests a structural sub-family (denominators in classes 0, 2 mod 3) that covers all large p — a candidate target.
first_step: Classify the surviving solutions by their mod-3 pattern; check if one pattern (e.g. two denominators ≡ 0 mod 3) suffices for p > 97 up to 10^6.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: xyz a perfect square: fails at 20 of 499 primes (13, 37, 97, 181, 193, 541, …)
connection: Requiring the product of the denominators to be a square is a 'quadratic' constrained world. Failures are sparse; 13, 37, 97, 193 are also hard in other worlds.
why: Square-product solutions correspond to rational points on a double cover of the ES surface (w² = xyz); this connects ES to a K3-like or del Pezzo double cover, where other tools (elliptic fibrations) exist.
first_step: Characterize: xyz = w² on 4xyz = p(xy+yz+zx) — find the parametric families producing squares; see whether failures fit a congruence.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Arakelov world: treat the archimedean bound x > n/4 as a degree condition on a metrized line bundle
connection: In FF, NC/degree conditions are degrees of divisors; over Spec Z compactified, positivity + size are Arakelov degrees. ES becomes: a metrized divisor class of degree log(n/4) is a 'sum' of three effective arithmetic divisors with unit-fraction structure.
why: Unifies the FF and Z worlds in one language so that FF proofs could be rewritten with Arakelov degrees and the failing step pinpointed (likely: Riemann–Roch for arithmetic surfaces is only asymptotic).
first_step: Write the FF proof of Lemma 1.1/1.3 in divisor language and attempt the Arakelov translation; note where h⁰ estimates are needed.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: One mute place (FF_MUTE Thm 3.5): ES_q^{(s)} is a theorem for every P via Bilharz–Weil — integer twin is Z[1/ℓ]
connection: FF_MUTE proves an FF variant with one 'mute' place s (denominators may have poles at s) for every P, effectively, using Bilharz's FF Artin theorem (RH). The integer twin is positive ES over Z[1/ℓ], which this lane shows holds for all odd ℓ < 3000 by an elementary Zsigmondy/reciprocity mechanism.

first_step: Write the FF_MUTE mechanism in the e | 1 + η language of other_rings Lemma 3.1 and compare with the Z[1/ℓ] proof; check whether an elementary FF proof also exists.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Ultraproduct of the Z[1/ℓ] proofs: uniform k ≤ 7 bound for ℓ < 3000 — is k bounded for all ℓ?
connection: The Z[1/ℓ] mechanism needed k ≤ 7 for all odd primes ℓ < 3000. If k is uniformly bounded, the statement is first-order uniform; if unbounded, the ultraproduct world (nonstandard ℓ) may fail the mechanism with standard k.
why: Uniform boundedness would be a clean elementary theorem; failure would show the mechanism's dependence on ℓ is genuinely arithmetic (Zsigmondy primitive divisors of growing order).
first_step: Extend the search to ℓ < 10^6 and track max k; try to prove k ≤ 3 or so for ℓ ≢ 1 (mod 8).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Signed FF world: ES_q with one 'negative' (leading coefficient −1) denominator
connection: Over F_q[T] (q odd) allow one denominator with leading coefficient −1. Like signed ES over Z this should be trivial via a telescoping identity; confirming the analogue strengthens the dictionary sign ↔ leading coefficient.

title: Transfer statement C (from F₂/F₄ finite coverings): 'signed covering + positivity repair'
connection: The |A| = 4 FF proofs are finite coverings using char-2 cancellation. Integer statement: a finite set of SIGNED identities covers all p, and for each p one can repair the sign using a second identity — i.e. ES ⇔ a 'repair' lemma for a finite signed covering.

first_step: Construct a finite signed covering of all p ≡ 1 (mod 4) by identities 4/p = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z with z ≫ p; formulate the repair condition explicitly.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Characteristic-p degeneracies of function-field ES (4 = 0 in char 2, 4 = 1 in char 3)
connection: Over F_{2^k}[T], 4/P = 0, so ES asks for three unit fractions summing to 0, which is P-independent and solvable (e.g. 1/T + 1/(T+1) + 1/(T(T+1)) = 0). Over F_{3^k}[T], 4/P = 1/P. These degenerations separate the role of the numerator 4 from the denominator's arithmetic.
why: Cheap sanity variants that test which function-field proofs use the size or arithmetic of the numerator 4 (and the 2-adic slot structure).
first_step: Work out ES over F_{3^k}[T]: is 1/P = 1/X + 1/Y + 1/Z with monic X, Y, Z always solvable, and by what identity?

connection: For n = 2 it fails (1/x + 1/y − 1/z < 2); for n ≥ 3 check solvability first, then count solutions in a box (z ≤ n²) and fit the same χ_p law. If the signed count follows χ_{−p} or χ_p with opposite sign, the sign structure of ES (SIGN_FIELDS.md) has a data signature.

connection: Relaxing integrality at 2 and 3 (S-integers) might make the odd-square obstruction disappear (T1 uses parity structure mod 4) and allow a complete identity cover; comparing the S-integral and integral problems isolates the role of the prime 2.

connection: Allowing one negative term is much easier (presumably always solvable by identities); the exact boundary between 'sign-mixed solvable by identities' and 'all-positive open' isolates what positivity costs.

connection: 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z with x,y,z ∈ ℤ[1/S]_{>0}. For S ∋ 2 this is much easier (more freedom). The ladder S = ∅ ⊂ {2} ⊂ {2,3} ⊂ … is the native 'S-integral points' relaxation of arithmetic geometry.
